reflection.quote: The days are long, but the years are short.
reflection.reading:
Sunday in mid-August has a particular texture. The summer is starting to lean toward its end, but it isn't over. There's still light in the evening. There's still time to do something with the day, or nothing at all. When I was drinking, Sundays were a write-off. Either I was hungover and hating myself, or I was already stacking the next round to soften the landing into Monday. I didn't know that Sundays could be their own thing.

What sobriety gave me — and this took years to appreciate — was the ordinary Sunday. Coffee that actually tastes like coffee. A slow walk. Texting a friend back. Making something for dinner instead of ordering it at 10pm because I forgot to eat. These are not thrilling. They are not the stuff of a highlight reel. But they are the raw material of a life you don't need to escape from.

Gretchen Rubin's line lands because it's true in both directions. A sober Sunday can feel long — especially early on, when the hours yawn open and you don't know what to do with them. But string enough of them together and you look up and realize you've built something. Eleven years of Sundays. Ski trips, quiet mornings, dinners with people who know your real name. The ordinary is where the years live.
reflection.meditation: What would it look like to let today just be a Sunday — not a problem to solve, not a day to get through, but a day to actually be in?

affirmations: I don't have to earn this day or fill it with anything spectacular — showing up sober is enough.
I am building a life out of ordinary hours, and those hours are mine.
Today I can choose rest, connection, or stillness without needing to numb any of it.

gratitude.prayer: I'm grateful for a Sunday I don't have to recover from. For the small stuff — clean sheets, a working body, people who text back. For the fact that the hardest years are behind me and the ordinary ones are here, and it turns out the ordinary is what I was actually looking for the whole time.
gratitude.closing: One more day. That's the whole thing.
